output.title: When glossary upkeep becomes overhead
output.body:
Glossary upkeep stops being useful when it no longer helps the same people answer the same operational question the same way.

If you run a small business, the check is simple: does the glossary reduce repeat questions, or has it turned into another document you now have to maintain?

That matters because not every recurring task deserves automation. Some work is frequent and repeatable. Some is just admin wearing better shoes.

A practical next step is to review the last week of repeated questions or term fixes and sort them into three buckets: keep as-is, merge into another workflow, or retire. If a term only needs a human judgment call once in a while, glossary upkeep may be the wrong place to spend attention. If it keeps changing how people answer customers, it still has a job.

For Bareni, that is the kind of bounded decision we look at: one recurring workflow, one clear rule, and human approval where the owner wants it. If the source material is paper-heavy or OCR-dependent, that is outside current scope and needs a different answer.
